    fix(simulation): restore flash cap and cycle-accurate spend in WASM core
    
    FLASH_WORDS was 65536 but the host loads at most 512 words, so the
    out-of-bounds trap never fired. spend() decremented remaining by 1
    regardless of the instruction's actual cycle cost, making multi-cycle
    instructions (RJMP, RCALL) consume only one cycle of budget.
    
    - Restore FLASH_WORDS to 512
    - spend(n) now subtracts n from remaining
    - Fix RJMP offset mask (0x07ff) and target (pc + k + 1) to match avr8js
    - Fix RCALL return address, target, and cycle cost (3, not 4)

# Parity scorecard — how close Noesis is to Wokwi and Velxio

Captured 2026-10-22 · parts pillar re-measured 2026-10-25 · measured at commit
`b2b4896` plus the environment-sensor slice · rubric v1 · the debugging pillar
re-measured 2026-10-26 after compiled AVR source-line debugging landed · the
parts pillar re-measured after the bus instruments, the shift register, the
matrix, the phone panel and the three environment sensors landed · the
ecosystem pillar re-measured after the simulation CI landed

**What this measures.** Two apps are the yardstick for this project: Wokwi,
because it is the closest thing to the product being built, and Velxio,
because it is the open-source rival with the same ambition and the same
component library underneath. "Parity" here means _a person who uses either
of them finds nothing in Noesis that stops them_ — not that Noesis is
identical to either, and not that it matches them in every particular.

**Method.** Eleven pillars, each weighted, each scored 0–100 against each
target. A pillar's score is a judgement about how much of that capability
Noesis has, against how much the target offers. Every score names the file
it was read from, so a reader can check it — and disagree with it — in the
same place. The weights are stated outright, because a different weighting
gives a different total and disagreement should be about the weights rather
than about arithmetic.

## The two targets, in brief

- **Wokwi** — 18 microcontrollers across AVR, ARM, RISC-V and Xtensa; ~62
  parts; real ESP-IDF firmware; GDB debugging; an 8-channel logic analyser at
  1 GHz that exports VCD to PulseView; a serial plotter; Wi-Fi simulation
  (MQTT, HTTP, NTP); SD-card simulation; a `.chip.wasm` custom-chip ABI;
  cloud projects; a VS Code extension; CI. ([docs.wokwi.com](https://docs.wokwi.com/))
- **Velxio** — 30+ boards on the free Maker plan and 40 on Pro, across 5 CPU
  families; 48+ components on the free canvas and 150+ across the full
  catalog; `arduino-cli` compilation; QEMU for the ESP32, STM32 and
  Raspberry Pi Linux boards; ngspice-WASM as the analog solver; C→Wasm custom
  chips and programmable sensors; 400+ example projects; docs in 9 languages;
  Docker self-hosting; an MCP server, an AI assistant, simulation CI and
  GitHub Sync. ([velxio.dev](https://velxio.dev/))

## The rubric

| #   | Pillar                            | Weight | What it covers                                                         |
| --- | --------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Firmware execution & CPU fidelity | 18%    | Whether the firmware that runs is the firmware you wrote               |
| 2   | Parts catalogue                   | 14%    | How many parts sit on the bench, and how many a sketch can talk to     |
| 3   | Electrical solver                 | 10%    | Whether the circuit is solved, and how faithfully                      |
| 4   | Board & architecture coverage     | 9%     | How many boards, how many CPU families                                 |
| 5   | Instruments                       | 9%     | Scope, logic analyser, meter, bus monitor, serial, plotter             |
| 6   | Curriculum & examples             | 10%    | Exercises, worksheets, worked examples, gallery                        |
| 7   | Persistence & sharing             | 7%     | Whether a circuit survives, travels, and can be handed to someone else |
| 8   | Debugging                         | 8%     | Breakpoints, stepping, variables, registers, GDB                       |
| 9   | Network & IoT                     | 5%     | Wi-Fi, HTTP, MQTT, NTP                                                 |
| 10  | Extension API                     | 5%     | Whether a user can add a part of their own                             |
| 11  | Ecosystem & workflow              | 5%     | VS Code extension, simulation CI, i18n, community, project README      |

Parts catalogue                   | 14%    | 55       | 52        | **78 bench-placed entries** — 61 named in `parts/catalogue.ts` plus 5 resistors, 4 capacitors, 5 LEDs and 3 pots — over **50 component kinds** (`parts/catalog.ts`), and every one of them a sketch can talk to. Four of the new entries are bus instruments with no element in the Wokwi library and no new firmware API: a **BMP180 barometer**, an **INA219 current monitor**, an **ADS1115 sixteen-bit converter** (`parts/devices/bmp180.ts`, `ina219.ts`, `ads1115.ts`), each speaking its own register protocol, and a **74HC595 shift register** on the SPI bus. A fifth is a **DS18B20** on one wire, answering through the `OneWire` library, a sixth is an **8x8 LED matrix behind a MAX7219**, a seventh is an **MFRC522 card reader**, the bench's first SPI device that answers — the bus now carries a byte back up MISO, so a sketch can read a register instead of only writing one — and an eighth is a **four-digit LED module behind a TM1637**, which is a new seam rather than a new bus: the chip's interface is two wires with no address, so the bench hands it whole transactions. A ninth is an **A4988 stepper driver**, the last of the eight named parts: it drives the motor's windings from a step pulse, the sketch never writes a phase table, and its five microstep modes are stamped as average bridge duties so the shaft can stop between full steps. A tenth is a **PCF8574 I/O expander**, which is what a project reaches for when the board has run out of pins: one byte over the I²C bus, and eight more. An eleventh is a **MAX6675 thermocouple**, the second device on the bench that answers over SPI and the first that answers with a measurement. A twelfth is an **MCP4725 converter**, the one part that drives a pin at a level of its own choosing: the bench could measure an analog level and now it can make one. A thirteenth is a **bench supply**, the only part whose voltage a person chooses — a second rail, so a motor can have the voltage it really wants. A fourteenth is a **24LC256 memory**, the bench's first device that is a pointer rather than a register file — sixteen-bit frames latched on the chip-select rise, and the first device on the bus that latches a whole frame rather than a byte. A seventh is a **Nokia 5110 behind a PCD8544**, whose command byte means one thing in the basic instruction set and another in the extended one. A fifteenth is a **DS3231 real-time clock**, which keeps the DS1307's BCD time registers and adds two alarms, a status flag that says whether the clock lost power, and a thermometer on the die. A sixteenth is an **MCP23017 I/O expander**, sixteen pins behind direction registers, so a sketch says which pins drive before a latch can move them. A seventeenth is a **PCA9685 PWM driver**, sixteen channels that switch rather than latch: each one compares a free-running counter against its own ON and OFF counts, so a sketch sets a duty and a phase, and the bench stamps the instantaneous waveform rather than an average. The environment bench adds three more, none of them in either target's part list: a **BH1750 light sensor**, a **TMP102 thermometer** and an **SHT31 temp/humidity sensor** (`parts/devices/bh1750.ts`, `tmp102.ts`, `sht31.ts`). They are deliberately not counted as three new capabilities: all three are I2C sensors on the existing `Wire` seam, and the protocols are the difference — one-byte commands with a continuous/one-shot choice, a pointer register with a signed twelve-bit word, and a sixteen-bit command whose six-byte answer carries a CRC after each measured word. The gallery's `environment-bench` and its diagnostics check read all three at once. That is why the score moves one point rather than three: the count is now above Wokwi's ~62, but the pillar still lacks the *kinds* of parts — motors, drivers and complex displays — that the targets carry. Wokwi lists ~62, of which the BMP180, the DS18B20, the 74HC595, the MAX7219 and the Nokia panel are five the bench now has; Velxio's two public figures disagree — 150+ parts across the catalog, 48+ on the free Maker canvas — and 62 sits between them. |

function i2cSensorDefinition(variant: I2cSensorVariant): PartDefinition {
  const module = I2C_MODULES[variant];
  return {
    id: module.id,
    name: module.name,
    category: 'input',
    widthMm: module.widthMm,
    heightMm: module.heightMm,
    component: { kind: 'i2c-sensor', device: variant },
    pins: headerPins(module),
    knobs: module.knobs,
    bodyColour: module.bodyColour,
    legendColour: module.legendColour,
  };
}

/** DS1307 real-time clock: the blue coin-cell module on a four-pin header. */
export function ds1307Definition(): PartDefinition {
  return i2cSensorDefinition('ds1307');
}

/** DS3231 real-time clock: the same header, with a thermometer on the die. */
export function ds3231Definition(): PartDefinition {
  return i2cSensorDefinition('ds3231');

  return i2cSensorDefinition('hx711');

Progress note:
The MCP23017 now answers a GPIO read from the wiring for every pin the sketch isn't driving, and the plan note that said otherwise is corrected.

**What changed**
- [mcp23017.ts](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts): the model gained an `Mcp23017PinLevels` sampler and `setPinLevels()`. A new `gpio()` builds the read byte bit by bit — an output bit reports its latch, an input bit reports the level the bench finds on the pin, and `IPOL` inverts the finished byte (so readback through polarity behaves as before). `OLAT` still reports the latch.
- [engine.ts](src/features/simulation/engine.ts#L599): the engine installs the sampler on every rebuild (the device is carried across rebuilds, the netlist is not), reading the port's net voltage against half the board's logic level. The `buildElements` comment that claimed inputs had "nothing wired to report" now states the real rule.
- Tests: four unit cases — wiring beats the latch, an unestablished pin reads low, a mixed byte consults the sampler only for input pins, and polarity inverts a wiring read — plus a live bench test that ties `PA0` to 3V3 and `PA1` to ground, then checks `GPIO_A`, `OLAT_A`, polarity, and a byte mixing a driven port with listening ones. The `i2cBench` test helper takes an optional `extra` hook to wire ports.
- [PLAN.md:377](docs/PLAN.md#L377): the paragraph now describes the per-pin read, the rebuild-installed sampler, and that an unwired port reads low.

**Verification**
- `mcp23017.test.ts` 12/12; `devices.test.ts` 44/44 (including the new live test).
- No regression in the existing project: gallery test "shows a sixteen-bit count on sixteen lights" passes, and `diagnostics/registry.test.ts` 6/6.
- `npm run typecheck` clean, `oxlint` 0 warnings/0 errors, `check:boundaries` ok (515 files).
- Limitations: the full suite is longer than this tool's 10-minute cap, so I ran the affected files instead; `oxfmt --check` reports issues on untouched files as well (CRLF), and it isn't part of `npm run check`, so I left formatting alone. Changes are uncommitted.

Two behaviours remain unmodelled on this chip and are worth knowing: its `GPPU` pull-up registers store but don't act, so an unwired input needs an external pull-up to read high, and interrupts stay inert.

Progress note:
The MCP23017's `GPPU` pull-ups now work as real resistors in the solve, so an input pin with its pull-up enabled sits at the supply when nothing external drives it — and still reads low when something ties it to ground.

**What changed**
- [mcp23017.ts](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts): added `pullUp(index)`, reading `GPPU_A`/`GPPU_B` (bank-0 `0x0C`/`0x0D`), plus `MCP23017_PULLUP_OHMS = 100_000` — the datasheet's typical value. The header docstring now says the pull-up registers act.
- [engine.ts](src/features/simulation/engine.ts#L2144): `buildElements` stamps a ~100 kΩ resistor from the port to its supply when the pin is an input with its pull-up enabled. Because it's a resistor rather than a forced reading, a wire to ground beats it, and an unwired pin is held at the rail by the chip itself.
- Tests: a unit case for the per-port pull-up bits (both banks, power-up all off) and a live bench case — pull-ups on `PA1` (wired to ground) and `PA3` (unwired) read `0b0000_1000`, then switching `PA3`'s pull-up off returns it to low.
- [PLAN.md:381](docs/PLAN.md#L381): the note now states `GPPU` stamps the chip's own ~100 kΩ into the solve, and why that makes a wire to ground win.

**Verification**
- `mcp23017.test.ts` 13/13 and `devices.test.ts` 45/45 pass.
- No regression for existing work: the gallery project "shows a sixteen-bit count on sixteen lights" still passes.
- `npm run typecheck` clean, `oxlint` 0/0, `check:boundaries` ok (515 files).

One detail worth knowing: only inputs get the pull-up stamped, matching the chip — a pin the sketch drives is push-pull and ignores the bit. Interrupts (`GPINTEN`, `INTCON`, the `INTF`/`INTCAP` registers) remain stored but inert, which is now the only unmodelled corner of this part.

The natural next step would be giving that inert half of the chip something to do.

Progress note:
The MCP23017's interrupt half now works end to end: the chip watches its pins, sets flags, and pulls INTA/INTB, which are real pins on the module.

**What changed**
- [mcp23017.ts](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts): added the interrupt registers — `GPINTEN` (0x04/0x05), `DEFVAL` (0x06/0x07), `INTCON` (0x08/0x09), `INTF` (0x0E/0x0F), `INTCAP` (0x10/0x11) and `IOCON` (0x0A/0x0B, aliased to one byte as the datasheet has it).
  - `updateInputs()` compares each watched pin every solve: `INTCON`=0 flags an edge against the previous level, `INTCON`=1 flags a level differing from `DEFVAL` (no baseline needed, so a pin already away from its default interrupts as soon as it's enabled). A hit ORs into `INTF` and latches the port byte into `INTCAP`.
  - `interruptLevel()` models the output stage: push-pull active-low by default, active-high with `INTPOL`, open-drain with `ODR` (which overrides the polarity and releases the pin instead of driving it high), and `MIRROR` moves port B onto INTA while INTB floats.
  - Reading `GPIO`, `INTF` or `INTCAP` clears the flag; writes to `INTF`/`INTCAP` are refused. The module gained `INTA`/`INTB` pins beside the bus header.
- [engine.ts](src/features/simulation/engine.ts#L2168): one `expanderPortLevel()` helper now feeds both readback and interrupt sampling so they can't drift; every solve samples the ports and stamps INTA/INTB as 1 kΩ push-pull outputs (or nothing when open-drain is released).
- Tests: seven new unit cases (no watch unless enabled, edge flag + capture, DEFVAL level mode, flag cleared by a port read, INTPOL polarity, open-drain release, mirror, read-only registers) and a live bench case that enables the pull-up on a watched port and sees INTA go low, the flag read `0x01`, then INTA release after the read.
- [PLAN.md:390](docs/PLAN.md#L390): documents the interrupt model; the old "stored but inert" sentence is gone.

**Verification**
- `mcp23017.test.ts` 21/21; `devices.test.ts` 46/46 (four live expander tests).
- Existing project unaffected: gallery "shows a sixteen-bit count on sixteen lights" passes, `diagnostics/registry.test.ts` 6/6.
- `npm run typecheck` clean, `oxlint` 0 warnings/0 errors, `check:boundaries` ok (515 files).

Two honest limitations remain: the `BANK` and `SEQOP` bits of `IOCON` are stored but don't change the register map (the model is bank 0 only), and interrupt flags are sampled once per solve, so a pulse shorter than the solver's step can be missed — real hardware has the same shape of problem, just at nanoseconds.

The obvious next step is showing this off in the gallery, since nothing there reads an interrupt yet.

 *
 * Each entry pairs a gallery id × build with the scripted checks that prove
 * the build still runs, plus a factory that wraps a real `Simulation` into a

 * `src/features/learn/gallery.test.ts` with identical tick counts and
 * margins; where a leg needs bench-deep access (`pushWokwiState` colon
 * sampling, the I2C bus log, LCD models, part knobs) the check asserts the
 * same behavior through the `HarnessSim` accessors instead, and the report
 * notes the substitution. The registry never touches the mounted bench,
 * editor state, or localStorage.

function verdict(name: string, started: number, status: CheckStatus, detail = ''): CheckResult {

function asProbe(sim: HarnessSim): ProbeSim {
  return {
    tick: (wallDeltaSeconds: number) => sim.tick(wallDeltaSeconds),

function sameGlyph(actual: readonly number[] | undefined, expected: readonly number[]): boolean {
  return (
    actual !== undefined &&
    actual.length === expected.length &&
    actual.every((value, index) => value === expected[index])

}

function sameGlass(
  actual: readonly (readonly number[])[],
  expected: readonly (readonly number[])[],
): boolean {
  return (
    actual.length === expected.length &&
    actual.every((glyph, index) => sameGlyph(glyph, expected[index]!))
  );
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ *
 * mcp23017 on uno: sixteen pins, one sixteen-bit number.

 * The expander's latches are its own state, so the check watches the lights
 * the two ports drive and compares them with the last number the sketch
 * printed -- sixteen bits, low byte on port A and high byte on port B.
 * ------------------------------------------------------------------ */

function mcp23017Checks(build: GalleryBuild): CheckDef[] {
  const leds =
    build.circuit.parts?.filter((part) => part.type === 'led-red').map((part) => part.id) ?? [];
  return [
    {
      name: 'the sixteen lights show the count the log reports',
      run: (sim) => {
        const started = performance.now();
        const name = 'the sixteen lights show the count the log reports';
        const read = sim.partVolts;
        if (read === undefined || leds.length !== 16) {
          return verdict(name, started, 'skip', 'the bench cannot read the lights');
        }
        for (let frame = 0; frame < 60; frame++) sim.tick(0.05);
        const counts = [...sim.serialText().matchAll(/count (\d+)/g)].map((match) =>
          Number(match[1]),
        );
        if (counts.length === 0) {
          return verdict(name, started, 'fail', 'the sketch did not report a count');
        }
        const value = counts[counts.length - 1]!;
        let wrong = 0;
        for (let bit = 0; bit < leds.length; bit++) {
          const isLit = read(leds[bit]!, 'anode') > 1;
          const shouldBeLit = ((value >> bit) & 1) === 1;
          if (isLit !== shouldBeLit) wrong += 1;
        }
        if (wrong > 0) {
          return verdict(
            name,
            started,
            'fail',
            `${wrong} of the ${leds.length} lights did not match the count`,
          );
        }
        return verdict(name, started, 'pass');
      },
    },
  ];
}

  if (projectId === 'pcf8574') return pcf8574Checks(build);

export function buildRegistry(): RegistryEntry[] {
  return GALLERY.flatMap((entry) =>
    entry.builds.map((build) => {
      const project = firmwareForBuild(build, boardOption(build.board).language);
      return {
        projectId: entry.id,
        buildLabel: build.variant === undefined ? build.board : `${build.board}:${build.variant}`,
        makeSim: makeSimFor(build, project),
        checks: checksFor(entry.id, build),
        // The AVR worker compile measures ~150 s, over the 120 s runner default.
        extendedCapMs:

  );

export interface RunOptions {

  readonly isCancelled?: () => boolean;
  readonly yieldEvery?: number;
  readonly wallCapMs?: number;
}

const DEFAULT_WALL_CAP_MS = 120_000;

function yieldToLoop(): Promise<void> {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}

async function withCap(
  result: Promise<CheckResult> | CheckResult,
  wallCapMs: number,
  name: string,
): Promise<CheckResult> {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  try {
    return await Promise.race([
      Promise.resolve(result),
      new Promise<CheckResult>((resolve) => {
        timer = setTimeout(
          () =>
            resolve({
              name,
              status: 'timeout',
              detail: `exceeded ${wallCapMs} ms`,
              wallMs: wallCapMs,
            }),
          wallCapMs,
        );
      }),
    ]);
  } finally {
    if (timer !== undefined) clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

/** A faulty check lands a fail row instead of rejecting the whole run. */
async function settleCheck(
  check: CheckDef,
  sim: HarnessSim,
  wallCapMs: number,
): Promise<CheckResult> {
  const started = performance.now();
  const fail = (error: unknown): CheckResult => {
    const detail = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error);
    return { name: check.name, status: 'fail', detail, wallMs: performance.now() - started };
  };
  let pending: Promise<CheckResult> | CheckResult;
  try {
    pending = check.run(sim);
  } catch (error) {
    return fail(error);
  }
  try {
    return await withCap(pending, wallCapMs, check.name);
  } catch (error) {
    return fail(error);
  }
}

export async function runHarness(
  checks: CheckDef[],
  makeSim: () => HarnessSim,
  opts: RunOptions = {},
): Promise<HarnessReport> {
  const yieldEvery = opts.yieldEvery ?? 1;
  const wallCapMs = opts.wallCapMs ?? DEFAULT_WALL_CAP_MS;
  const started = performance.now();
  const sim = makeSim();
  const results: CheckResult[] = [];
  let done = 0;
  for (const check of checks) {
    if (opts.isCancelled?.() === true) {
      results.push({ name: check.name, status: 'skip', detail: 'cancelled', wallMs: 0 });
      continue;
    }
    const result = await settleCheck(check, sim, wallCapMs);
    results.push(result);
    done += 1;
    opts.onProgress?.(done, checks.length);
    if (done % Math.max(yieldEvery, 1) === 0) await yieldToLoop();
  }
  const wallMs = performance.now() - started;
  const simMs = readSimMs(sim);
  const ticks = readSimTicks(sim);
  return {
    projectId: '',
    buildLabel: '',
    results,
    metrics: { wallMs, simMs, ratio: simMs / Math.max(wallMs, 1), ticks },
  };
}

export function formatReport(report: HarnessReport): string {
  const fps = report.metrics.wallMs > 0 ? report.metrics.ticks / (report.metrics.wallMs / 1000) : 0;
  const lines = [
    `${report.projectId} (${report.buildLabel}): ${report.results.filter((r) => r.status === 'pass').length}/${report.results.length} pass`,
    `wall ${report.metrics.wallMs.toFixed(0)} ms, sim ${report.metrics.simMs.toFixed(0)} ms, ratio ${report.metrics.ratio.toFixed(2)}, fps ${fps.toFixed(1)}`,
  ];
  for (const result of report.results) {
    lines.push(
      `[${result.status}] ${result.name} (${result.wallMs.toFixed(0)} ms)${result.detail === '' ? '' : ` — ${result.detail}`}`,
    );
  }
  return lines.join('\n');
}

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ *
 * One pin, sixteen inputs — the expander does the watching
 * ------------------------------------------------------------------ */

const EXPANDER_INTERRUPT: GalleryProject = {
  id: 'expander-interrupt',
  title: 'One Pin, Sixteen Inputs',
  blurb:
    'A button sits on an MCP23017 port, and the expander watches it itself. When the button moves the chip pulls INTA, so the sketch reads one pin it already has instead of asking the expander over I²C on every pass of loop().',
  parts: [
    { name: 'I/O expander (MCP23017)', qty: 1 },
    { name: 'Tactile Button', qty: 1 },
    { name: 'Red LED', qty: 1 },
    { name: '220 Resistor', qty: 1 },

    {
      board: 'uno',
      libraries: [],
      sketch: `#include <Arduino.h>
#include <Wire.h>

/*
 * Sixteen pins on two wires, and one more wire for the interrupt.
 *
 * The sketch tells the expander which port to watch and then leaves: the
 * chip samples PA0 itself and pulls INTA low when it moves. That turns a
 * decision the sketch would have to poll for into a level it can read with
 * one digitalRead.
 *
 * The pull-up is the chip's own, switched on with GPPU, so the button only
 * has to connect the port to ground. It is switched on and allowed to settle
 * before the pin is watched, because a pin coming up is an edge too.
 */
const byte EXPANDER = 0x20;
const byte IODIR_A = 0x00;
const byte INTCON_A = 0x08;
const byte GPPU_A = 0x0C;
const byte INTF_A = 0x0E;
const byte GPIO_A = 0x12;
const byte GPINTEN_A = 0x04;
const int INTA_PIN = 2;
const int LED_PIN = 8;

byte readRegister(byte address) {
  Wire.beginTransmission(EXPANDER);
  Wire.write(address);
  Wire.endTransmission();
  Wire.requestFrom(EXPANDER, 1);
  return Wire.available() ? Wire.read() : 0;
}

void writeRegister(byte address, byte value) {
  Wire.beginTransmission(EXPANDER);
  Wire.write(address);
  Wire.write(value);
  Wire.endTransmission();
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(INTA_PIN, INPUT);
  pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);
  Wire.begin();

  writeRegister(IODIR_A, 0xFF);   // PA0 is an input
  writeRegister(INTCON_A, 0x00);  // any change is an interrupt
  writeRegister(GPPU_A, 0x01);    // the chip supplies the pull-up
  delay(10);
  readRegister(INTF_A);           // the pull-up coming up is not a press
  writeRegister(GPINTEN_A, 0x01); // now watch PA0

  Serial.println("watching PA0");
}

void loop() {
  // One read of one pin, instead of a bus transaction per pass.
  if (digitalRead(INTA_PIN) == LOW) {
    // Reading the port clears the flag and says which way the button went.
    byte port = readRegister(GPIO_A);
    if ((port & 0x01) == 0) {
      digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);
      Serial.println("pressed");
    } else {
      digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
      Serial.println("released");
    }
  }
  delay(5);
}

The interrupt half of the chip is modelled too. `GPINTEN` names the pins to
watch, and the engine samples every port once per solve, so an edge is seen
between transactions rather than only when a sketch reads. `INTCON` chooses
what counts: a zero flags a change from the level the pin held last time, and
a one flags a pin that differs from `DEFVAL`, which is a level rather than an
edge -- a pin already away from its default is an interrupt the moment the
sketch asks for one. A flag set in `INTF` also captures the port into
`INTCAP`, and reading `GPIO`, `INTF` or `INTCAP` takes the flag down, the way
the chip does. The two outputs are stamped like the ports are: push-pull and
active low by default, active high with `INTPOL`, open-drain with `ODR` (which
overrides the polarity and releases the pin rather than driving it high), and
`MIRROR` puts both ports on INTA and leaves INTB alone.

```
  writeRegister(GPINTEN_A, 0x01); // now watch PA0
```

Should I adjust the comment to explain the port read is the reference? "the first port read is the reference" is accurate for the chip; on the bench the model doesn't use a read reference. Maybe keep it simpler: "// settle the pin before watching it: no press". But the reason for reading GPIO specifically is to clear any flag and set the reference. In the model it clears any flag. Let me write:

```
  readRegister(GPIO_A);           // reading the port clears any start-up flag
  writeRegister(GPINTEN_A, 0x01); // now watch PA0
```

## Clean-path redirect, now for every top-level page

[main.tsx](src/main.tsx) now matches prefixes instead of a single path: `/boards`, `/learn`, `/projects`, `/bench`, `/diagnostics` — and anything beneath them (`/learn/0.1`, `/projects/uno`, `/bench/nano`), since the router still decides what the rest of the path means. The rewrite still happens before React mounts via `history.replaceState`, so no history entry is added and the hash router reads it as its initial location.

One route gap had to be closed for this to be true rather than nominal: `/projects` had no route of its own (`/projects/:boardId` only), so a clean link would have been folded into `#/projects` and then bounced home by the catch-all. [App.tsx](src/app/App.tsx) now has a `/projects` route that redirects to the default board, exactly as `/bench` already did.

**Verified in the running app** (dev server on 5188):

| Link typed | Lands on | Heading |
|---|---|---|
| `/boards` | `#/boards` | "Pick the board you would like to use." |
| `/learn/references` | `#/learn/references` | "Reference & glossary" |
| `/projects` | `#/projects/uno` | "Arduino Uno R3" |
| `/bench` | `#/bench/uno` | bench renders (187 SVG parts) |
| `/diagnostics` | `#/diagnostics` | "Smoke-test the gallery", 29 rows |
| `/nope` | stays `/nope` → home | unchanged, as before |

`npm run typecheck` clean, `oxlint` 0 warnings/0 errors on both files. Same limitation as before: this rescues a clean path only where the host serves `index.html` for it — a static host without a rewrite still 404s before the app loads.

## Learnings saved to AGENTS.md

There was no root `AGENTS.md`, so I created [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) with four sections, all terse:

- **A gallery project touches five places, not one** — circuit JSON plus registration, the `GALLERY` entry, a live leg in `gallery.test.ts`, and a checks function in `diagnostics/registry.ts`; the coverage test in `registry.test.ts` fails a project without checks, and the doc counts are hand-maintained.
- **The diagnostics harness reads pins by definition id** — `partVolts(id, 'anode')`, never the circuit's `A`/`K` alias, which returns 0 V silently; and checks in one entry share a sim, so later ones may rely on earlier state.
- **No `attachInterrupt`** — the interpreter refuses it by design; edge demos watch the part's INT pin with `digitalRead`.
- **Verification here** — the full suite outruns the 10-minute cap (run changed files instead), `format:check` fails repo-wide on CRLF and isn't a gate, and routes are hash-based with `main.tsx` folding clean paths in.

Everything remains uncommitted, and the dev server is still running on port 5188 with the panel as the thread preview. Saved learnings only reach future sessions when the **AGENTS.md** option in the composer settings menu is enabled.

I've reviewed the whole uncommitted change against the MCP23017 datasheet and probed the model directly. **Nothing was fixed**; the working tree is exactly as it was, and my temporary probes were deleted.

## Verdict

The wiring is sound — circuit registered, gallery project listed, diagnostics entry wired, counts correct, all checks green. But the interrupt model diverges from the real chip in three places, and one of them is now taught by the new sketch.

## High — reading `INTF` clears the interrupt, but the chip doesn't do that

[mcp23017.ts:321](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts#L321) zeroes the flag when `INTF` is read. The datasheet says the opposite: *"The interrupt remains active until the INTCAP or GPIO register is read"*, and `INTF` is read-only. My probe confirms the model's behaviour — the flag read `0x01` and `interruptLevel(0)` went from asserted (`false`, pin low) to released (`true`, pin high) after that single read.

What this breaks:
- A sketch that polls `INTF` to find the source silently releases INTA in the sim; on hardware the interrupt stays asserted until it reads the port.
- The new demo's setup guard, [gallery.ts:2306](src/features/learn/gallery.ts#L2306) `readRegister(INTF_A); // the pull-up coming up is not a press`, is a **no-op on hardware**. It only works on the bench because of this bug. The datasheet-correct idiom is to read `GPIO_A` once after the pull-up settles, which both clears the flag and sets the comparator's reference. (The model also compares consecutive solves rather than the value latched by the last port read, so whether a real chip would report a phantom boot press is worth a hardware check — but the comment as written teaches a mechanism the chip doesn't have.)
- The behaviour is baked into [mcp23017.test.ts:114](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.test.ts#L114) (expects `0x02` on the second read; hardware would show `0x03` because flags persist) and [PLAN.md:395](docs/PLAN.md#L395) ("reading `GPIO`, `INTF` or `INTCAP` takes the flag down").

## High — `MIRROR` releases INTB instead of driving it

[mcp23017.ts:267](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts#L267) returns `null` for port B when mirrored, and the engine stamps no element, so INTB floats. The datasheet's `MIRROR` bit is *"1 = The INT pins are internally connected"* — both pins carry the interrupt, which is why breakouts let you use either. A mirror-mode circuit wired to INTB will never see an interrupt in the sim, and it fails silently (the pin just sits at whatever else holds it).

Encoded in [mcp23017.test.ts:158](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.test.ts#L158) ("INTB is not driven when mirrored") and [PLAN.md:399](docs/PLAN.md#L399) ("leaves INTB alone"). Both need to change with the fix.

## Medium — driven pins are treated as a frozen input in the interrupt path

[mcp23017.ts:216](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts#L216): for a pin the chip drives, `now` takes the *previous sampled* bit, which is initialised to 0 and never changes. The comment says "its level is the latch", but the code doesn't use th

[...truncated 2614 chars...]

t only writes its ports, so the readback change doesn't alter it.
- ODR/INTPOL semantics match the datasheet ("Open-drain output (overrides the INTPOL bit)").
- `git diff --check` clean; `registry.test.ts` 6/6; typecheck, oxlint and boundaries clean. The full suite wasn't run (AVR compile legs exceed the tool cap).

## Before you commit

Two files are untracked and must be added: [expander-interrupt.json](src/features/learn/circuits/expander-interrupt.json) and [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). Committing `circuits/index.ts` without the JSON leaves a broken import.

The three model bugs are the ones worth fixing before this goes on GitHub — the gallery project and its checks pass today, but they pass partly because the model is wrong in the same direction as the sketch.

# AGENTS.md

Working notes for this repo. Everything here is something the code does not tell
you on its own, or costs an hour to rediscover.

## A gallery project touches five places, not one

Adding a `GalleryProject` is never a single-file change: a circuit document in
`src/features/learn/circuits/` plus its registration in `circuits/index.ts`, the
`GALLERY` entry with its sketch, a live bench leg in `gallery.test.ts`, and a
checks function in `diagnostics/registry.ts` wired into `checksFor`.

The diagnostics entry is not optional: `diagnostics/registry.test.ts` asserts
every gallery build has at least one check, so a project without one fails the
suite even though the project itself runs. That same file also has to list the
project id before its checks are executed rather than merely counted.

Counts are hand-maintained in `docs/parity-scorecard.md` (gallery projects,
committed circuits) and the part paragraphs in `docs/PLAN.md`; a new project or
part will leave them stale unless you update them.

## The diagnostics harness reads pins by definition id

`HarnessSim.partVolts(partId, pinId)` looks the pin up in the netlist, which
uses the part definition's ids (`anode`, `cathode`), not the circuit JSON's
wire aliases (`A`, `K`). Passing an alias returns 0 V rather than throwing,
so a check looks like "the light never came on".

Checks in one entry share a single sim and run in order, so a later check may
depend on state an earlier one built — the existing entries already do this.

## Sketch constraint: no attachInterrupt

The interpreter refuses `attachInterrupt` on purpose. A demo that needs an edge
must either poll, or watch the part's own INT pin with `digitalRead` and touch
the bus only when it fires — that is the idiom the MCP23017 project uses.

## Verification in this environment

`npm test` (the whole suite) outruns a 10-minute command cap because of the AVR
compile legs. Verify with `npx vitest run <changed paths>` instead; `npm run
check` is the full gate when there is no cap.

`npm run format:check` fails across the repo on CRLF line endings and is not
part of `npm run check`. It is not a gate; do not reformat files to satisfy it.

Routing is hash-based (`/#/boards`, `/#/diagnostics`). `src/main.tsx` folds the
clean top-level paths into the hash before the router mounts, but a static host
without a rewrite rule still answers a clean path with its own 404.

These are not directly comparable execution architectures. Wokwi’s public documentation describes a digital MCU simulator with limited analog I/O; Velxio’s public repository describes a hybrid system that adds an ngspice-based analog solver, but also runs some MCU emulators on a backend. **There is no controlled, apples-to-apples performance benchmark in the sources reviewed, so the architectural differences below should not be read as a speed ranking.**

| Runtime factor | Wokwi | Velxio |
|---|---|---|
| **MCU emulation** | Wokwi’s open-source [AVR8js library](https://github.com/wokwi/avr8js) is a JavaScript AVR CPU implementation; the project says it accepts precompiled machine code and leaves peripheral simulation to its host application. Wokwi’s [AVR8js technical introduction](https://blog.wokwi.com/avr8js-simulate-arduino-in-javascript/) describes instruction-by-instruction execution and a cycle counter. Wokwi’s [RP2040js repository](https://github.com/wokwi/rp2040js) likewise documents a JavaScript Pico emulator. For ESP32, Wokwi documents supported chips, peripherals and a speed-related CPU-frequency cap, but the sources reviewed do **not** disclose the simulator’s underlying CPU engine or execution-thread placement. | The [Velxio repository](https://github.com/davidmonterocrespo24/velxio) and its [architecture document](https://github.com/davidmonterocrespo24/velxio/blob/master/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) describe AVR and RP2040 execution in the browser, and QEMU-based backends for ESP32-family boards and Raspberry Pi Linux. Its [RP2040 technical note](https://github.com/davidmonterocrespo24/velxio/blob/master/docs/RP2040_EMULATION.md) specifies a `requestAnimationFrame` loop at about 60 FPS, batching CPU cycles per frame, plus a WFI fast-forward path that skips ahead during waits instead of executing idle cycles. That note says 125 MHz; the repository overview also says 133 MHz, so the published clock figures are inconsistent. |
| **Worker, threading and location** | Public Wokwi docs and the AVR8js source establish browser-compatible JavaScript emulation, but do not establish whether Wokwi’s current product runs each simulator in a Web Worker. For other targets, including ESP32, the reviewed public docs do not disclose enough to make a threading comparison. | Velxio’s browser-board paths are documented as frame-loop emulation; the reviewed architecture does not document a separate browser Worker for those paths. Its ESP32 backend is different: the [ESP32 technical note](https://github.com/davidmonterocrespo24/velxio/blob/master/docs/ESP32_EMULATION.md) describes QEMU on the backend, with QEMU initialization and its main loop kept on the same daemon thread. The frontend exchanges simulation events over WebSocket. Thus “browser-based” describes the UI, not necessarily where every board’s CPU executes. |
| **Analog simulation / co-simulation** | Wokwi’s [Analog API documentation](https://docs.wokwi.com/chips-api/analog) explicitly describes Wokwi as a digital simulator with “very limited analog simulation.” It documents voltage readings and outputs, including examples such as potentiometers and thermistors—not a general circuit-level SPICE solve. Wokwi’s GitHub organization also has an [ngspice-WASM build repository](https://github.com/wokwi/ngspice-wasm), but that alone is not evidence that Wokwi’s simulator integrates it; the product’s Analog API is the relevant description of its documented analog capability. | Velxio’s [architecture document](https://github.com/davidmonterocrespo24/velxio/blob/master/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) specifies a lazy-loaded ngspice-WASM engine, netlist generation from the wired circuit, MCU pins represented as Thevenin sources, and solved voltages made available to instruments and ADC reads. The same document describes electrical solving as debounced work during simulation. This is a materially different capability, with a corresponding potential runtime cost that depends on the circuit and solve workload. The repository verifies the integration approach; claims such as “SPICE-accurate” are not accompanied there by independent accuracy or performance benchmarks. |
| **Rendering and UI work** | The [Wokwi Elements repository](https://github.com/wokwi/wokwi-elements) says its web components provide presentation, not functional hardware simulation. The reviewed Wokwi sources do not document a rendering-performance threshold, a worker-based renderer, or a comparable component-count benchmark. | Velxio’s architecture describes React/TypeScript UI, Wokwi Elements plus Velxio-native web components, and SVG wire paths. Its architecture document lists WebGPU acceleration for canvases above 200 components as **planned**, not a current performance feature. Neither project provides a comparable rendering benchmark in the material reviewed. |
| **Compilation and startup** | In Wokwi’s [VS Code project configuration](https://docs.wokwi.com/vscode/project-config), firmware is built by the user’s toolchain and then loaded by the simulator; an ELF file is optional and the docs say it can speed simulation in some cases. The [VS Code getting-started guide](https://docs.wokwi.com/vscode/getting-started) also tells users to compile before simulating. These docs do not give current compile-latency or cache figures for Wokwi’s hosted editor. A Wokwi [2019 AVR8js blog post](https://blog.wokwi.com/avr8js-simulate-arduino-in-javascript/) describes a cloud compilation service, but that historical description should not be treated as a current timing or implementation guarantee. | The repository describes compilation through a FastAPI backend using `arduino-cli` and ESP-IDF. Its README documents persistent build directories and `ccache` for ESP-IDF, and gives project-maintainer estimates ranging from **5–7 minutes without retained caches after a restart** to seconds for cached/incremental builds. Those are repository-reported scenarios, not independent benchmarks; actual results depend on the board, cache state, server and project. |

### What matters most in practice

- **For analog circuits interacting with firmware**, Velxio’s documented ngspice co-simulation is the clearest architectural difference. It also adds solver work and a lazy-loaded bundle—the architecture document estimates about 39 MB—so it is not a free performance feature. Wokwi documents analog voltage I/O and modeled parts, not a general SPICE network solver.
- **For execution cost, board choice matters in Velxio.** Its AVR/RP2040 paths run in the browser, while ESP32 and Raspberry Pi Linux paths use backend QEMU and a WebSocket bridge. The RP2040 WFI optimization avoids simulating long idle waits, but does not establish a general runtime speed for CPU-intensive firmware.
- **Wokwi documents a specific ESP32 speed control:** its [ESP32 guide](https://docs.wokwi.com/guides/esp32) says the default `cpuFrequency` is `auto`, capping simulated CPU frequency at about 8 MHz to achieve higher simulation speed; it says this does not change peripheral timing. Setting `cpuFrequency` to `max` is documented as making simulation much slower. This is a stated simulator policy, not a benchmark against Velxio.
- **Do not infer all-client execution from Velxio’s marketing language.** Its [About page](https://velxio.dev/about/) uses “100% in your browser” language, while the technical repository explicitly documents server-side QEMU for some boards. For execution location, the repository’s board-specific technical notes are the more precise source.
- **No defensible overall performance winner follows from these sources.** Wokwi does not publicly specify enough of its current ESP32 internals or rendering/thread model for that comparison, and neither project publishes matched benchmarks. The verified differences are capabilities and architecture—not measured end-to-end speed."}]}

Fix the three MCP23017 divergences from the datasheet: INTF reads must not clear the interrupt, MIRROR must drive both INT pins, and driven pins must not take part in interrupt flags while INTCAP carries their latch.

---

Progress note:
Fixed. The model, the gallery sketch and the docs now agree with the datasheet.

**1. Reading `INTF` no longer acknowledges the interrupt** ([mcp23017.ts:321](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts#L321))
The flags register is now pure readback; only `GPIO` or `INTCAP` clears the flag, matching *"the interrupt remains active until the INTCAP or GPIO register is read"*. Writes to `INTF`/`INTCAP` remain refused.

**2. `MIRROR` drives both INT pins** ([mcp23017.ts:264](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts#L264))
Removed the `return null` for port B. With `MIRROR` set, `interruptLevel(0)` and `interruptLevel(1)` return the same level, so the engine stamps both pins — the datasheet's "internally connected" rather than "INTB floats".

**3. Driven pins are out of the interrupt path, and their latch is captured** ([mcp23017.ts:211](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.ts#L211))
- A pin the chip drives now contributes its **latch** to the sampled port byte instead of a frozen previous sample, so `INTCAP` carries the same value a port read would show (`0b1111_0001` in the probe that used to report `0b0000_0001`).
- `GPINTEN` is masked with `IODIR`, so a bit set for an output does nothing — no edge and no `DEFVAL` hit. The probe that forced `INTF = 0b1111_0000` on driven pins now reads `0x00`.

**The demo follows the chip's idiom now** ([gallery.ts:2305](src/features/learn/gallery.ts#L2305))
The setup read `INTF_A` only because of the old bug; it now reads `GPIO_A` once after the pull-up settles, which is what actually clears a start-up flag and sets the comparison level on hardware. The unused `INTF_A` constant and the comment claiming the read only clears a flag were removed.

**Tests**
- [mcp23017.test.ts](src/features/parts/devices/mcp23017.test.ts): DEFVAL now expects the accumulated `0x03` (flags persist across an `INTF` read); the mirror test expects both pins asserted; three new cases — "leaves the interrupt up when the flags register is read", "does not flag a pin the chip is driving", "captures a driven pin from its latch".
- [devices.test.ts:659](src/features/parts/devices/devices.test.ts#L659): the live test now reads `INTF` and asserts INTA **stays** asserted, then reads the port and asserts it releases.
- [PLAN.md:395](docs/PLAN.md#L395) states the corrected clearing rule, the latch in `INTCAP`, the input-only interrupt sources, and the tied mirror pins.

**Verification**
- `mcp23017.test.ts` 24/24, `devices.test.ts` 46/46, the gallery leg passes, `registry.test.ts` 6/6.
- The Diagnostics panel still reports `expander-interrupt (uno): 2/2 pass` after the change.
- `npm run typecheck` clean, `oxlint` 0 warnings/0 errors, `check:boundaries` ok (515 files).

Two things from the review are deliberately untouched because they're outside this request: the wrong pin-id example in [AGENTS.md:25](AGENTS.md#L25) (`K` is a label, the id is `cathode`), and the one `oxfmt` line wrap in [registry.ts:1621](src/features/learn/diagnostics/registry.ts#L1621).

# AGENTS.md

Working notes for this repo. Everything here is something the code does not tell
you on its own, or costs an hour to rediscover.

## A gallery project touches five places, not one

Adding a `GalleryProject` is never a single-file change: a circuit document in
`src/features/learn/circuits/` plus its registration in `circuits/index.ts`, the
`GALLERY` entry with its sketch, a live bench leg in `gallery.test.ts`, and a
checks function in `diagnostics/registry.ts` wired into `checksFor`.

The diagnostics entry is not optional: `diagnostics/registry.test.ts` asserts
every gallery build has at least one check, so a project without one fails the
suite even though the project itself runs. That same file also has to list the
project id before its checks are executed rather than merely counted.

Counts are hand-maintained in `docs/parity-scorecard.md` (gallery projects,
committed circuits) and the part paragraphs in `docs/PLAN.md`; a new project or
part will leave them stale unless you update them.

## The diagnostics harness reads pins by definition id

`HarnessSim.partVolts(partId, pinId)` looks the pin up in the netlist, which
uses the part definition's ids (`anode`, `cathode`), not the circuit JSON's
wire aliases (`A`, `K`). Passing an alias returns 0 V rather than throwing,
so a check looks like "the light never came on".

Checks in one entry share a single sim and run in order, so a later check may
depend on state an earlier one built — the existing entries already do this.

## Sketch constraint: no attachInterrupt

The interpreter refuses `attachInterrupt` on purpose. A demo that needs an edge
must either poll, or watch the part's own INT pin with `digitalRead` and touch
the bus only when it fires — that is the idiom the MCP23017 project uses.

## Verification in this environment

`npm test` (the whole suite) outruns a 10-minute command cap because of the AVR
compile legs. Verify with `npx vitest run <changed paths>` instead; `npm run
check` is the full gate when there is no cap.

`npm run format:check` fails across the repo on CRLF line endings and is not
part of `npm run check`. It is not a gate; do not reformat files to satisfy it.

Routing is hash-based (`/#/boards`, `/#/diagnostics`). `src/main.tsx` folds the
clean top-level paths into the hash before the router mounts, but a static host
without a rewrite rule still answers a clean path with its own 404.

## Short answer

Focus first on **measuring the bottleneck**, then improve **simulation throughput** and **solver scaling**. Noesis already has several performance foundations—worker-based simulation, shared-memory snapshots, cached solves, reused matrix buffers, and idle-time skipping—so I wouldn’t start by moving everything to WebGPU or rewriting the simulator in Wasm.

I reviewed the current diff and surrounding code; the uncommitted changes are documentation/formatting only, not performance changes. **I made no edits.**

## Highest-value opportunities

1. **Make performance comparisons repeatable.**  
   The existing [Wasm performance test](src/features/simulation/avr/wasm-perf.test.ts) times 20 ticks of one alarm-clock workload, but its assertion only verifies that the run took nonzero time. Use a small set of representative circuits—CPU-heavy, display-heavy, and analog-heavy—and report warm-run p50/p95 for **simulated seconds per wall second**, solver calls and iterations, frame time, and compile-to-run time. That will show whether the next fix belongs in the CPU backend, solver, or UI.

2. **Offer a measured throughput mode, separate from real-time pacing.**  
   The worker advances a fixed simulated-time slice on each 16 ms interval, with a 40 ms cap in the core ([worker.ts](src/features/simulation/sim-worker/worker.ts#L19), [core.ts](src/features/simulation/sim-worker/core.ts#L148)). A configurable “real time” versus “run as fast as practical” mode could improve CPU-heavy runs while keeping the UI responsive. Preserve simulated-time semantics for delays and peripherals; this is an explicit speed-versus-fidelity choice, not a free optimization. Wokwi documents a related tradeoff: its ESP32 “auto” CPU frequency is capped around 8 MHz to speed simulation without changing peripheral timing ([Wokwi ESP32 docs](https://docs.wokwi.com/guides/esp32)).

3. **Target solver scaling if profiling confirms it dominates.**  
   The analog solver uses dense LU and refactors the matrix during Newton iterations ([circuit.ts](src/features/simulation/circuit.ts#L1), [matrix.ts](src/features/simulation/matrix.ts#L1)). It already reuses scratch buffers, and the engine caches identical solves ([engine.ts](src/features/simulation/engine.ts#L1578)); don’t spend effort redoing those wins. The larger opportunity is exploiting circuit sparsity—reuse the matrix’s structural pattern and use sparse numeric factorization as circuits grow. There’s useful evidence in the solver’s own notes: on the alarm bench, widening the diode linearisation step from 0.25 V to 3.5 V reduced recorded iterations per settle from 30.6 to 5.1 ([circuit.ts](src/features/simulation/circuit.ts#L20)). That suggests solver work can be a substantial cost, but benchmark broader circuits before taking on a more complex solver.

4. **Speed up repeated compile/run cycles.**  
   The AVR toolchain assets already have an IndexedDB cache, and some exact project sources have prebuilt HEX. I didn’t find a general cache for arbitrary user-project build results: compiling a project creates a worker for the build and terminates it afterward ([toolchain client](src/features/simulation/avr/toolchain/client.ts#L445)). Caching successful results by source, board/core, libraries, and toolchain version—and reusing a warm worker where safe—could make unchanged reruns much quicker. Velxio’s README also describes persistent build caches; it reports browser-board simulation at about 60 FPS and documents an RP2040 wait-for-interrupt optimization ([Velxio README](https://github.com/davidmonterocrespo24/velxio)). Those are first-party claims and implementation notes, not an apples-to-apples speed test.

## Already in good shape

Noesis already skips waits when the circuit has no dynamics ([engine.ts](src/features/simulation/engine.ts#L1408)), offloads simulation through a worker and shared memory, and limits React rendering to roughly 30 FPS while continuing to poll the worker ([Bench.tsx](src/features/bench/components/Bench.tsx#L850)). Velxio’s documented wait-for-interrupt behavior is therefore not an obvious missing optimization here. If visual smoothness is the specific complaint, measure the render path before raising the 30 FPS cap; more frequent full paints could compete with the simulation.

There’s no reliable public, apples-to-apples benchmark establishing that either competitor is faster for the same circuit and firmware. I’d start with the benchmark suite, then use its results to choose between scheduler, solver, compile, or rendering work.

A useful next step would be to build a repeatable benchmark suite for the simulator.
why do we need benchmark?

Because “performance” can mean very different things here: firmware instructions per second, circuit-solver time, compile wait, or UI smoothness. A benchmark helps identify which one is actually limiting the experience, so improvements target the cause instead of adding complexity to the wrong part.

For example, the existing test separates CPU time from solver time for one workload, but it isn’t a robust comparison across circuits. A small representative set would help prioritize work and verify that a change made the intended part faster without slowing another. If your goal is only to brainstorm likely improvements, we can skip benchmarking and choose a focused area based on your current priorities.
my current priority is to have a fast running simulation

Got it. I’d focus on **how quickly the simulation advances**, not on matching competitors feature-for-feature. The UI already redraws at about 30 FPS, while the simulation runs in a worker, so raising the render rate probably isn’t the first lever ([Bench.tsx](src/features/bench/components/Bench.tsx#L850)).

The clearest throughput constraint is the worker’s pacing: it tries to step every 16 ms, and the simulation core caps each step at 40 ms ([worker.ts](src/features/simulation/sim-worker/worker.ts#L19), [core.ts](src/features/simulation/sim-worker/core.ts#L148)). That limits the current fast-forward approach: increasing its multiplier beyond the cap won’t keep increasing simulated time per tick.

**My first choice would be a “run as fast as practical” mode:** let the worker do several simulation steps in a bounded chunk, then yield so it can process controls and the UI can read an updated snapshot. Keep the current real-time mode for users who want hardware-like pacing. The tradeoff is that fast mode uses more CPU and needs to preserve the solver’s fine-grained timing for PWM, probes, and other time-dependent behavior.

After that, I’d reduce snapshot work if it shows up as a cost, then tune the circuit solver if measurements show it dominates. Existing optimizations already skip static delays and avoid redundant solves, so I wouldn’t start by rewriting those paths.

A small before/after throughput check would help confirm the fast mode actually improves simulated time per wall-clock time; it doesn’t need to become a broad benchmarking project. I can sketch the fast-mode behavior and its timing/fidelity tradeoffs next.

can we utilize GPU to run the simulation?

Yes, technically—**WebGPU compute** could run parts of the simulation on the GPU. But for Noesis’s current workload, it probably wouldn’t be the first route to a faster-running simulation.

The firmware emulators and circuit-solving steps have dependencies between operations, while the circuit matrices are typically small. Moving data to the GPU and coordinating each step could cost more than the GPU saves. The UI is already rendered through the browser’s graphics stack; GPU compute wouldn’t speed up React’s work rebuilding or updating the bench.

GPU compute becomes more promising if Noesis needs to solve **many circuits in parallel**—for example, parameter sweeps—or if circuit sizes grow substantially. For faster single-circuit runs, I’d first focus on worker pacing and CPU-side hotspots in the solver or firmware execution ([simulation worker](src/features/simulation/sim-worker/worker.ts), [circuit solver](src/features/simulation/circuit.ts)). A small measurement can tell us which of those matters most without turning this into a broad benchmark project.
